candidate.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential; monitor trends in physiologic data, recognize worsening hemorrhage, and integrate quantitative findings with clinical assessment
candidate.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — quantitative and cumulative blood-loss monitoring in postpartum hemorrhage
candidate.educational_objective: Track postpartum hemorrhage with quantitative and cumulative blood-loss assessment while active bleeding continues, and interpret the trend together with maternal vital signs and clinical status rather than relying on visual estimation or a single number alone.

options.A: Use quantitative methods when feasible and maintain a cumulative blood-loss record while active bleeding continues, integrating the trend with the client’s vital signs and overall clinical condition.
options.B: Rely on visual estimation alone because it is generally more accurate than quantitative measurement when blood loss becomes large.
options.C: Record only the first blood-loss estimate and stop cumulative assessment even if active bleeding continues.
options.D: Use the quantified blood-loss value as the sole determinant of severity and ignore signs of hypovolemia or other clinical deterioration.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. ACOG states that quantitative measurement of obstetric blood loss is more accurate than visual estimation and that implementation includes both direct quantitative measurement and protocols for collecting and reporting a cumulative blood-loss record after delivery. ACOG also notes that ongoing blood-loss assessment should continue while active bleeding is present and that blood-loss values must be interpreted together with clinical findings such as signs of hypovolemia. B reverses the evidence because visual estimates can substantially under- or overestimate blood loss. C can miss continued accumulation. D is unsafe because clinical deterioration may be important even when a numeric threshold alone is not decisive.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Quantitative blood-loss measurement is more accurate than visual estimation; cumulative blood loss should be tracked and reported during ongoing postpartum bleeding and interpreted alongside the client’s clinical condition.
candidate.source_document_title: Quantitative Blood Loss in Obstetric Hemorrhage; Postpartum Hemorrhage Practice Bulletin No. 183
candidate.source_locator: Committee Opinion No. 794 Recommendations and Conclusions — quantitative methods are more accurate than visual estimation; implementation includes direct measurement and protocols for collecting/reporting a cumulative postdelivery record. Processes for Quantification — ongoing assessment suggested while active bleeding is present; obstetric nurses play a critical role in tracking quantitative and cumulative blood loss. ACOG PPH definition incorporates cumulative blood loss and signs/symptoms of hypovolemia
